lines.note: Riun denotes victory or triumph. The example begins Riunuo fi-, continuing the verb hiraku below; it is the word anticipated by f421’s catchword.
Raqu completes hiraku, with uru as an alternative. The Portuguese gives triumphing or gaining victory.

runs.text: Filha de lagarto de q̃ falão os gẽtios.

lines.note: Ryūnyo is the dragon’s daughter in the source’s account of non-Christian belief. The printed circumflex in Riûnho is retained rather than changed to the carons found in neighboring entries.
Ryūnō is camphor; Baiqua names an especially fine kind. The scan shows a circumflex over u and a caron over o, giving Riûnǒ rather than OCR Riùnǒ.
Fora completes can-fora, characterized as very good and excellent. The physical division is preserved.

runs.text: Laya, ou feição em couſas de arte.

lines.note: Ryūryū is a manner or style in artistic work. Both u vowels in the printed headword bear carons.
Te ni ryūryū ga aru concerns varieties of style in handwriting. The example repeats riǔriǔ, correcting OCR nuriǔ; the Portuguese translation begins with Na letra.

runs.text: talho, ou feição. ¶ Item, Ramos, ou va-

lines.note: Talho and feição complete the handwriting-style explanation. A further sense begins: branches or varieties of religious schools.
Riedade completes va-riedade, finishing the sense of differing sects or schools. It is not a separate headword.
Ryūsui is flowing water, nagaruru mizu. The historical mizzu spelling and long s in the headword are retained.

runs.text: Raiz de hũa certa erua, que ſerue de

lines.note: Ryūtan is the root of a certain herb used medicinally. The Portuguese explanation is kept without adding a species identification.
Mezinha completes the statement of medicinal use. This short continuation belongs to the preceding root entry.
Ryūtei means weeping or lamentation. The example begins Riǔtei co-, with its initial R upright rather than absorbed into the italic paragraph apparatus.
Garuru completes kogaruru in the weeping example. The Portuguese describes drying up from tears; the printed wording is preserved.
Ryūō is king of the dragons, given explicitly as Riǔnouǒ. The headword reads Riǔuǒ, replacing OCR Rihuǒ without modernizing the source’s u/o notation.
Ryūsha is a carriage, kuruma, described as swift or in motion. The source abbreviates que as q̃.
Andando completes the moving-carriage definition. It remains separate from the following meteor entry.

runs.text: Exalação que ſe acende denoite no ar,

lines.note: Ryūsei is explained historically as an exhalation igniting in the night air. The scan restores Riǔxei and acende, rather than OCR Fibxei and aceinde.
The phenomenon appears like a flying star. This is the source’s historical description, not a modern physical explanation.
Ryūshi means the willow’s threads, yanagi no ito. The Portuguese identifies the slender branches that are described further below.

runs.text: ſalgueiros que estão de pendurados como fios.

lines.note: The branches hang like threads. The upright S. marks written usage rather than belonging to the botanical gloss.
Ryūshoku is the color of willow, yanagi no iro. The whole headword is upright; final S. is a separate usage label.
Ryūyō concerns discharging a debt by an agreed substitute or indirect payment. Tate mochiyuru is the printed Japanese paraphrase; the Portuguese explanation continues across several rows.

runs.text: algũa couſa da diuida, ou toda conforme ao de

lines.note: The debtor may discharge part or all of the debt, according to the creditor’s wish. Couſa replaces OCR conſa; the row ends de without an invented division mark before ſejo.

runs.text: ſejo do acredor, em algũa couſa q̃ não ſeia a meſ

lines.note: Sejo completes deſejo, the creditor’s wish. Payment may be made in something other than the original loan; meſ continues into ma without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: ma q̃ ſe emprestou, ou pagãdo por via de outro

lines.note: Ma completes meſma. The explanation also permits payment through another person; the provisional st in emprestou is retained rather than globally reclassified.

runs.text: ainda q̃ ſeja ameſma prata ẽ eſpecie, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Even the same kind of silver may be repaid through that intermediary. Printed ameſma remains joined, and Vt introduces the example.

runs.text: Icquã meno cauarini coreuo riǔ yô tçuca

lines.note: The example offers this item in place of one kanme. The scan shows the abbreviation Icquã and a printed space in riǔ yô; tçuca continues into matçuru on the next row.

runs.text: Deu, ou pagou iſtoẽ troco dos cẽ taeis

lines.note: Matçuru completes the deferential verb. The Portuguese says it was given or paid in place of a hundred taels: enlargement favors cẽ, not OCR dẽ. The initial c is damaged, so this chosen reading retains a small degree of uncertainty. The joined iſtoẽ remains unexpanded.

runs.text: Aſas, ou orelhas dos ſinos de Iapão

lines.note: Ryūzu are the handles or suspension loops of Japanese bells. The Portuguese uses the anatomical metaphors “wings” and “ears.”

runs.text: por onde estão de pendurados, que commummẽ

lines.note: These are the loops from which the bells hang. Commummẽ continues into te on the next row, without an invented hyphen.

runs.text: te tem figura de hum lagarto.

lines.note: The loops commonly take a dragon-like form, described in Portuguese as a lagarto. This completes the bell-fitting definition.
Risei means governing the realm, yo wo osamuru. The Portuguese divides impe-rio across the physical line boundary.

runs.text: rio, ou reino em paz, & com ordem.

lines.note: Rio completes imperio; the gloss specifies governing a kingdom peacefully and in order. S. is upright.
The second Risei means intellectual keenness and sagacity. The example begins Rixeina, wholly upright rather than partly italic.
Hito completes the example of an acute and discerning person. The Portuguese diſcreto is retained in its historical character-description sense.

runs.text: O dar, ou empreſtar dinheiro à õzena.

lines.note: Risen is lending money at interest, expressed by à õzena in the source. The historical financial gloss is transcribed without modernizing the term or its tilde.
Rishō is benefit, favor, or reward from Camis and Fotoques. The headword’s initial R is upright; Camis is a Japanese designation embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Gorishō ni azukaru means receiving such favor or benefit. Re- begins the Portuguese verb on the next row; Fotoques remains a term within the gloss.

runs.text: ceber a graça, ou fauor dos Camis, ou Fotoques.

lines.note: Completes receber as receiving grace or favor from the Camis or Fotoques. Both embedded terms are flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Risshin is establishing oneself, mi wo tatsuru, by adopting a livelihood or station. The row ends vi, with the i visible, not OCR v.

runs.text: da, ou eſtado de maneira que ſe ſostente, & fi

lines.note: Da completes vida, and the chosen state should sustain the person and leave him well established. The row ends fi without a supplied hyphen before que.
Que completes fique; bem encabeçado finishes the description of being securely established. This line closes the preceding livelihood entry.
Risshū marks the beginning of autumn, tatsu aki. The historical seasonal expression is preserved without imposing a modern calendar date.
Risshun marks entering or beginning spring, haru tatsu. The Portuguese word is divided primaue-/ra.
Completes the spring definition. The printed joined aprimeuera and its vowel sequence are retained rather than normalized.
Riyaku is saving or delivering people, hito wo sukuu. The Portuguese Oſaluar is closely set as in the supplied draft.
Os homẽs completes the people being saved. The nasal abbreviation is retained and the physical row remains separate.

runs.text: Proueito, ou intereße proprio que hum

lines.note: Riyō is personal profit or advantage. The entire Japanese headword is upright, including initial R, rather than partly italic as in the draft.

runs.text: procura ſem ter deuer com o dos outros. Vt,

lines.note: The definition specifies pursuing one’s own interest without regard for others. Vt introduces the example that follows.
Myōmon riyō wo honto su makes reputation and self-interest the principal aim. The printed joined fonto is retained.

runs.text: cõ hiprocreſias, & ſeu proueito, ou intereße.

lines.note: The Portuguese describes seeking reputation hypocritically and pursuing one’s own advantage. The scan supports hiprocreſias, with an i missing from OCR; the unusual printed spelling is not modernized.

runs.text: Cubiça, ou ſer amigo de ſeu proueito.

lines.note: Riyoku is greed or attachment to one’s own profit. The Portuguese gives both the abstract vice and a personal disposition.
Riyoku wo kamayuru is illustrated as being intent on one’s own advantage. The Japanese example stays upright.
Completes the example as being self-interested or covetous. It belongs to the preceding sentence rather than the next entry.

runs.text: O apertar, ou conuencer com re-

lines.note: Rizzume means pressing or convincing with reasons. The Portuguese verb is conuencer with historical consonantal u, not OCR contencer; re- continues below.
Zões completes rezões. Rizzumeni ſuru repeats the sense as a verbal construction; its initial R is upright.
The new alphabetical section begins with RO and a two-line enlarged R. Alporcas names the swellings; Roga deqita illustrates their appearance. The Portuguese begins printed Na-, not OCR Ne.
Cerão completes the source’s Na-/cerão spelling in the preceding example. No unprinted s is inserted to make a modern form.
A different Ro is illustrated by ro no koromo, a thin garment. The Portuguese explanation continues with who wears it.

runs.text: que trazem os Bonzos por cima.

lines.note: The thin garment is worn over other clothing by Buddhist monks. This completes ro no koromo, rather than defining the next homograph.
Ro is an oar. Ro wo osu is glossed simply as rowing; the printed voſu is retained.

runs.text: Solda com que pegão, ou ſoldão hum

lines.note: Rō is solder used to join one metal to another. The scan restores ſoldão where OCR broke the word into ſo dão.
Completes the joining of metals and introduces rōzuke wo suru, to solder. The example begins Rǒzzuqeuo with R, not OCR A.
Zer completes Fa-zer, followed by “this soldering.” It belongs to the preceding example.
A separate Rō means wax. Its Japanese headword is wholly upright; the italic R in the draft was spurious.
Another Rō concerns fatigue, tsukaruru. Rō wo tsumu begins an example of accumulating exertion or hard work.

runs.text: Trabalhar muito, ou ter muito traba-

lines.note: Mu completes tsumu. The Portuguese describes much work, or having worked greatly, with traba- continuing below.

Lhado completes trabalhado. The next example is rō shite kō nai gi ja, labor without useful result; the scan supports n in cônaigui, rather than OCR u. The narrow separation before gui is not decisive, so the draft’s single-word spacing is retained.

runs.text: Depois de canſar, & trabalhar não a-

lines.note: Gia completes the Japanese predicate. The Portuguese says that after tiring oneself and working one gains no benefit.

runs.text: proueitar, nem aquirir virtude, ou mere-

lines.note: Completes aproveitar and adds failing to acquire virtue or merit. The historical aquirir is retained without inserting d.
Cimento completes merecimento. The following rō ga iku is separately glossed as becoming tired.
Rô, paraphrased by Yagura, denotes a bulwark or tower. The example Rôni nobo- continues with ru on the next physical line; both Japanese initials are roman, not isolated italic letters.

runs.text: Subir aeſta torre. Mais frequẽtemẽte ſe

lines.note: The continuation completes noboru, to climb, and translates the example as climbing this tower. Mais frequẽtemẽte introduces the explanation of its more usual occurrence in compounds on the next line.

The explanation says that this word is used in compounds and gives Cǒrô, a high tower. The scan reads vſa, not the draft voſca, and Torre has two r letters. The first vowel after p is not entirely clear, so the draft’s unusual polaura is retained. The supplied st allograph in cõposta is also retained rather than normalized.
Alta, &c. completes the Portuguese explanation of Cǒrô as a high tower. This short continuation belongs to the tower entry, not the following prison entry.
This separate Rô means a prison. Rôuo qeyaburu introduces breaking the confinement by kicking; its Portuguese translation breaks physically at Que- and continues on the next row.

runs.text: brar o tronco com os pès. ¶

lines.note: Brar completes Quebrar, and the Portuguese specifies breaking the stocks or confinement with the feet. Rôni iruru begins the next example, to put someone in prison; the Japanese initial belongs to the roman phrase.
Encarcerar translates Rôni iruru as imprisoning someone. Rôyori idaſu then means to bring someone out of prison, with Tirar introducing the Portuguese continuation.
Alguem do tronco completes the translation of releasing someone from confinement. Tronco is retained as the printed Portuguese term, rather than replaced by a modern word for prison.
Roba denotes an ass or donkey; the Portuguese explicitly includes both male and female animals. Its short first vowel distinguishes this entry from the long-vowel Rǒba entries below.
Rǒba is paraphrased as Voitaru vma, an aged horse, matching Caualo velho. The caron on the first vowel is retained, as is initial v in vma.
This Rǒba is instead Voitaru vba, an old woman. The difference between vma on the preceding row and vba here is semantically significant and is supported by their different Portuguese definitions.

Rǒba xinxet is glossed by Nengorona cocoro, an affectionate or solicitous disposition. The Portuguese Grã- continues as de on the next line, introducing great love and favor; no modernized Japanese spelling is substituted.

runs.text: de amor, & fauor. ¶ Item, Se toma por

lines.note: De completes Grãde, describing great love and favor. The following paragraph sign and Item introduce an additional, unfavorable sense whose definition continues below.
Couſa prolixa, & enfadonha supplies the additional sense: something long-winded and tiresome. This completes the Rǒba xinxet entry rather than constituting a new headword.
Rǒbiǒ denotes illness associated with old age. The initial is R rather than the draft B; the Portuguese reads Doẽça, with an abbreviation over e, rather than Docça.
Rǒbo, paraphrased as Voita faua, means an aged mother. The scan-supported historical faua is retained rather than replaced by modern haha, and the Portuguese is Mãy velha.
Rǒbocu, with Voita qi, means an old tree. Qi is the dictionary’s spelling for the Japanese word for tree; Aruore velha independently confirms the sense.
Rǒbu is explained as Voitaru chichi, an aged father, matching Pay velho. The longer Voitaru is retained in contrast to Voita in the two preceding explanations.
Rǒca means a passageway or corridor. The compact Portuguese Paßadiço retains the printed double-s character rather than being normalized to a modern spelling.

Rôcacu, glossed by Yagura, iye, denotes tall houses or buildings, compared with those belonging to high-ranking people. The roof-shaped accents are retained here, unlike the carons in the preceding old-age entries.

The Portuguese completes the comparison with houses of lords and nobles: nobres, not the draft nolbres. Rôcacu tamauo starts a Japanese example continuing beyond this page; its remaining text is not supplied as body text from the catchword.
